rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four real desks, not three variations on the same business-model question. Its "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" and "What runners actually give up when the shoe belongs to the brand" add supply-chain and runner-experience paths B never finds. B's "Can a profitable public company make money renting out a shoe it grinds up?" is a clever question, but without fee, margin impact, or materiality it is mostly an analyst note hunting for a spreadsheet.
gaps_in_A: "this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" overstates what the update proves; the return trigger could be mileage, time, or subscriber choice, and A correctly lists that as proof it still needs.
"The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" risks making a trend out of one national program unless On can provide volume, sourcing, or supplier proof.
"mailing it back is a condition of the deal" needs contract-term proof before a reporter can safely write it that strongly.
gaps_in_B: "Can a profitable public company make money renting out a shoe it grinds up?" is not yet a markets story; there is no fee, margin impact, guidance, analyst note, or materiality proof in the update.
"subscription economics actually work" in angle one and "whether this helps or dilutes margins" in angle three are too close; B pads the business-model lens instead of finding another protagonist.
B misses two cleaner distinct desks: the castor-bean materials/supply-chain angle and the runner/customer-experience angle.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is the wrong workflow call; this needs proof gathering and journalist-fit-check before a draft roast.
